lessons.title: T1.01 — Where Am I Now?
lessons.objectives: Diagnostic + goal setting across speaking, listening/note-taking, reading and writing. Output: baseline self/major introduction, short written response, mini synthesis, confidence/goal survey. No grade.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.01 — Where Am I Now? — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Quick pair exchange: name, major, one English success from the past year.
Output challenge: Cold attempt: 60–90 second self/major introduction. Teacher records only observable evidence, not a grade.
Targeted noticing/input: Show the four pathway descriptions and the nine UENG outcomes. Students identify which two matter most to them now.
Guided practice: Run the short reading and listening baselines; model how to record notes without writing full sentences.
Production 1: Students complete the writing baseline and select pathway + target.
Feedback: Students compare their own confidence rating with what the four tasks actually showed. Teacher avoids converting the diagnostic into a score.
Improved attempt: Repeat the opening introduction with one improvement: clearer structure, one concrete example and a closing goal.
Exit ticket: One sentence: The English task I most need to improve is ___ because ___.
lessons.homework: 10 minutes: enter or draft your pathway, year target and one piece of baseline evidence to keep for the end-of-year comparison.

lessons.title: T1.02 — Read With a Purpose
lessons.objectives: Skim, scan, predict, identify structure, claims and evidence. Output: explain the most important message from a university-level text and identify supporting evidence.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.02 — Read With a Purpose — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.01, recall one personal goal and turn it into a reading purpose: What information would help me with this goal?
Output challenge: Give students 45 seconds to answer: What is this text mainly doing? No dictionaries and no sentence-by-sentence translation.
Targeted noticing/input: Model the difference between topic, purpose, claim and supporting evidence using one paragraph.
Guided practice: SQ3R mini-cycle: survey headings/shape, ask two questions, read, recite the answer from memory, review against the text.
Production 1: Pairs prepare a 45-second explanation of the main message plus the strongest supporting evidence.
Feedback: Listeners use two checks only: Did I hear the message? Did I hear evidence from the text?
Improved attempt: Students explain again in 30 seconds with no paper, keeping only three key words.
Exit ticket: Write one reading move you used today and when you would use it again.
lessons.homework: 12 minutes: take any short English text from your major and mark purpose, one claim and one piece of evidence. Bring only the marked text or a photo.

lessons.title: T1.03 — Listen and Capture Meaning
lessons.objectives: Listen for structure, signposting and keywords; organise notes and reconstruct meaning. Output: 60-second explanation using notes only.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.03 — Listen and Capture Meaning — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Without notes, reconstruct the four-part structure from T1.02: problem, evidence, response, limitation.
Output challenge: Play/read the script once. Students may write only eight words total. Ask: What changed, and what did not change?
Targeted noticing/input: Highlight spoken signposts: first, then, the important point, if. Show how signposts predict note structure.
Guided practice: Read again in chunks. Students reorganise notes into Situation / Change / Action rather than chronological transcription.
Production 1: Students deliver the 60-second update from notes only.
Feedback: Partners tick three items: accurate main message, logical order, no reading full sentences.
Improved attempt: Teacher removes one minute of preparation. Students give a 30-second executive version.
Exit ticket: Write the one keyword or symbol that helped you recover the most meaning.
lessons.homework: 10 minutes: listen to any 1–3 minute English explanation once and make notes using headings + keywords only. Write a 2-sentence reconstruction.

lessons.title: T1.04 — Say It in Your Own Words
lessons.objectives: Summary, paraphrase, quotation, attribution, patchwriting and academic integrity. Introduce responsible AI use. Output: transform a short source into an accurate concise explanation.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.04 — Say It in Your Own Words — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.03, reconstruct a message from only three keywords. Connect that compression skill to summarising.
Output challenge: Show the three sample paraphrases. Students vote: safe / risky / inaccurate, then justify one choice.
Targeted noticing/input: Mini-model: preserve meaning first, then change structure and wording; quotation marks for exact words; attribution for borrowed ideas.
Guided practice: Students transform one sentence in three steps: identify meaning units → close source → rewrite → reopen and verify.
Production 1: Students produce the summary, paraphrase and short quotation task.
Feedback: Peer check uses four questions: same meaning? new structure? clear attribution? any invented claim?
Improved attempt: Students revise the weakest item and add a one-line note: what changed and why.
Exit ticket: Complete: A paraphrase becomes inaccurate when ___.
lessons.homework: 15 minutes: choose one short paragraph from a course source. Write a 50-word paraphrase and add a 2-line verification note comparing it with the original.

lessons.title: T1.05 — Make Data Speak
lessons.objectives: Charts, trends, comparison, quantity, cautious interpretation and avoiding unsupported causal claims. Output: 90-second major-relevant data explanation.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.05 — Make Data Speak — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Recall the distinction from T1.04 between what a source says and what a writer adds. Apply it to charts: observation vs interpretation.
Output challenge: Show only the three data series. Students get 60 seconds to choose the single most important message.
Targeted noticing/input: Model weak vs strong language: ‘X caused Y’ versus ‘X changed while Y…; this may suggest…, but…’.
Guided practice: Pairs build one sentence for trend, comparison, uncertainty and next action.
Production 1: 90-second data explanation to a new partner.
Feedback: Listener writes the speaker’s main message. If it differs from the speaker’s intended message, the explanation needs redesign.
Improved attempt: Give the same update in 45 seconds, leading with the headline.
Exit ticket: Write one claim the data supports and one claim it does not support.
lessons.homework: 10 minutes: find or create a small dataset from your major (3–6 values). Write a headline sentence plus one cautious interpretation.

lessons.title: T1.06 — Build an Argument
lessons.objectives: Claim → reason → evidence → qualification/counterpoint; distinguish fact, evidence, interpretation, opinion and assumption. Output: short evidence-supported position.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.06 — Build an Argument — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Use T1.05 language to separate observation from interpretation in one evidence card.
Output challenge: Students choose yes/no/conditional in 20 seconds, then must defend the choice with one evidence card.
Targeted noticing/input: Teacher models an argument with a strong claim but weak evidence, then one with qualification.
Guided practice: Small groups sort statements into fact, evidence, interpretation, opinion and assumption; discuss disputed items.
Production 1: Pairs deliver 75-second positions followed by one counter-question.
Feedback: Partner checks whether every major claim has a reason/evidence link and whether the qualification is genuine.
Improved attempt: Switch sides and give a 45-second version of the opposing case.
Exit ticket: Write the assumption in your own argument that most needs checking.
lessons.homework: 12 minutes: take one claim from your major or campus life. Add one reason, one piece of evidence you would need, and one qualification.

lessons.title: T1.07 — Source-Based Position
lessons.objectives: Major assessed performance 1. Use a short reading/listening source set to deliver an approximately two-minute evidence-supported position, then revise after feedback.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.07 — Source-Based Position — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: One-minute recall: claim–reason–evidence–qualification from T1.06.
Output challenge: Before support, students listen/read once and state a provisional answer in one sentence.
Targeted noticing/input: Clarify assessment evidence: understanding, evidence, reasoning, organisation, language clarity and qualification.
Guided practice: Students fill the source grid, select only evidence that directly supports their position and rehearse with a partner.
Production 1: Two-minute source-based position.
Feedback: Use the linked rubric. Give one strength and one priority for revision; avoid correcting every language error.
Improved attempt: 60–90 second revised attempt targeting the priority.
Exit ticket: Write exactly what you changed between attempt 1 and attempt 2.
lessons.homework: No new content. Spend 10 minutes saving the first/revised evidence and your feedback priority in the portfolio.

lessons.title: T1.08 — Academic Discussion
lessons.objectives: Enter and manage discussion: invite, agree/disagree, qualify, ask for evidence, clarify and repair misunderstanding. Output: structured small-group academic discussion with distributed speaking time.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.08 — Academic Discussion — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Recall one qualification phrase from T1.06/T1.07 and use it in a 20-second warm-up opinion.
Output challenge: Silent individual allocation first; groups then discover where opinions conflict.
Targeted noticing/input: Model three bad discussion habits: waiting, interrupting, agreeing without reasons. Students repair each one with a language function.
Guided practice: Triads rehearse entry, invitation, clarification and disagreement in 30-second micro-rounds.
Production 1: 8-minute budget discussion with role rotation and an action/decision record.
Feedback: Observers track contribution distribution and mark one moment where clarification improved the decision.
Improved attempt: Groups run a 3-minute ‘executive version’ with one new condition: the budget falls by 25%.
Exit ticket: Who helped the discussion move forward today, and what exactly did they do?
lessons.homework: 10 minutes: write five useful discussion phrases from memory, then compare with the linked language bank and correct them.

lessons.title: T1.09 — Explain Your Major to Me
lessons.objectives: Audience adaptation. Explain a process, concept, technology, model or idea from the student's major to an intelligent non-specialist. Output: 2–3 minute explanation.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T1.09 — Explain Your Major to Me — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.03, give a 30-second update with only headings. Transfer the same ‘structure before detail’ principle to explanation.
Output challenge: Students explain their item for 45 seconds with no preparation. List where listeners become lost.
Targeted noticing/input: Teacher demonstrates jargon dumping versus audience-aware explanation. Students identify exactly what makes the second version clearer.
Guided practice: Students map specialist terms to plain definitions/examples and rehearse one difficult step.
Production 1: 2–3 minute major explainer to a mixed-major partner/group.
Feedback: Listeners write one sentence explaining the concept back. Misunderstanding becomes feedback evidence.
Improved attempt: Students repair the least clear 30–45 seconds and answer one new question.
Exit ticket: Write one piece of assumed knowledge you removed from your explanation.
lessons.homework: 15 minutes: make one simple diagram or 5-step outline for your explainer. No paragraph slides.

lessons.title: T1.10 — Present Clearly
lessons.objectives: Opening, signposting, sequencing, transitions, conclusion, vocal delivery, slide discipline and audience attention. Output: 3-minute mini-presentation without reading paragraphs from slides.

lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Retell the structure of your T1.09 explainer without content: purpose → parts/steps → example → importance.
Output challenge: Show a deliberately overloaded slide and ask pairs to redesign it in 90 seconds using only six visible words plus one visual concept.
Targeted noticing/input: Model vocal emphasis and pause placement on the same sentence; identify how delivery changes meaning.
Guided practice: Students rehearse opening + transition + conclusion only before filling the middle.
Production 1: 3-minute presentation in groups; one student times, one listens for structure, one listens for delivery.
Feedback: Two-column feedback: message/structure and delivery/visuals. One priority only in each.
Improved attempt: Repeat the opening and weakest transition/conclusion immediately.
Exit ticket: Write the sentence you want the audience to remember tomorrow.
lessons.homework: 15 minutes: revise your mini-presentation to a clean 3–5 slide version and keep the before/after slide as portfolio evidence.

lessons.title: T1.11 — Combine Sources
lessons.objectives: Synthesis rather than separate summaries; compare reading and listening using agreement, contradiction, addition, limitation and qualification. Output: integrated spoken or written synthesis.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.

lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.04, state the difference between summary and paraphrase. Add: synthesis answers ‘how do sources relate?’
Output challenge: Students hear/read both sources once and write one sentence beginning ‘Taken together…’.
Targeted noticing/input: Compare two paragraphs: source-by-source summary versus idea-by-idea synthesis. Students highlight relationship language.
Guided practice: Pairs sort six source statements into agreement, addition, tension or limitation.
Production 1: Write/speak the synthesis without copying full source phrases.
Feedback: Partner underlines relationship language and circles any sentence that could be written from only one source.
Improved attempt: Revise so every sentence either combines sources or has a clear reason to focus on one.
Exit ticket: Complete: Synthesis is different from two summaries because ___.
lessons.homework: 12 minutes: find two short English sources on one topic from your studies. Write three bullet relationships only—no full summary.

lessons.title: T1.12 — Can I Trust This?
lessons.objectives: Evaluate authorship, evidence, date, relevance, source type, unsupported claims and AI-generated information. Output: verify claims and explain the reasoning behind each verdict.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.

lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.05/T1.06, give one example of a claim that goes beyond evidence.
Output challenge: Display the precise unsupported statistic first. Ask: What makes a claim feel trustworthy even when we have not verified it?
Targeted noticing/input: Separate source credibility from claim support: a credible source can still be outdated or irrelevant; an AI answer can be useful but is not its own evidence.
Guided practice: Teams inspect the five simulated source cards and defend one disputed verdict.
Production 1: Each student produces a verification log for two claims and explains one verdict orally.
Feedback: Partner challenges the weakest link: author, evidence, date, relevance or independent confirmation.
Improved attempt: Student upgrades one verdict by stating the next check they would actually perform.
Exit ticket: Write the sentence: ‘I would not trust this yet because…’ using a concrete reason, not ‘because it is AI.’
lessons.homework: 15 minutes: take one factual claim from an AI answer or online source you encounter. Preserve the claim, record one independent check, and note whether your confidence changed.

lessons.title: T1.13 — Explain China Across Cultures
lessons.objectives: Intercultural explanation without stereotyping. Recognise assumed knowledge, define unfamiliar concepts, compare, clarify and avoid over-generalisation. Output: international-audience explainer + follow-up questions.

lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.09, list two kinds of assumed knowledge that can make an explanation fail.
Output challenge: Students explain one familiar Chinese/campus item in 30 seconds. Listener interrupts at the first unexplained assumption.
Targeted noticing/input: Repair absolute language: ‘Chinese students…’ → ‘In many universities / in this situation / some students…’.
Guided practice: Pairs annotate an explanation for hidden assumptions, unexplained names and unnecessary comparison.
Production 1: 2-minute international-audience explainer + questions.
Feedback: Listener reports what they understood and one question caused by missing context rather than language.

Exit ticket: What did you know so well that you forgot your audience might not know it?

lessons.title: T1.14 — Integrated Academic Challenge
lessons.objectives: Combine research/input, source evaluation, evidence, discussion, explanation, structured output and response to questions. Revision/rehearsal for final performance.

Feedback: Listener writes the research question they heard. Writer checks whether it matches the intended one.
Improved attempt: 30-second revised pitch leading with the clarified question and significance.
Exit ticket: Write your research/project question in one sentence without vague nouns like ‘development’ or ‘application’ unless defined.
lessons.homework: 15 minutes: revise the pitch outline and contact message after feedback. Keep both versions as evidence.

lessons.title: T2.15 — Take Your Local Expertise Global [FLEX]
lessons.objectives: FLEX. Explain something meaningful from JUST, Zhangjiagang, Suzhou/Jiangsu industry, Chinese innovation, trade or the student's discipline to an international audience.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.

Linked lesson kit: T2.15 — Take Your Local Expertise Global [FLEX] — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Recall T1.13’s hidden-assumption checklist and T2.07’s system-explanation structure.
Output challenge: Give only the local name/topic to a partner. Partner lists what they would need explained before the significance makes sense.
Targeted noticing/input: Teacher models ‘name-dropping local context’ versus explaining why the listener should care.
Guided practice: Students build an audience knowledge gap list and choose only the context needed to close it.
Production 1: 2-minute explainer + one sceptical/clarifying question.
Feedback: Listener identifies one local detail that became globally understandable and one remaining assumption.
Improved attempt: Repair the most local/opaque 30 seconds.
Exit ticket: Which local term/name needed the most context, and what definition worked?
lessons.homework: Optional FLEX follow-up: turn the explainer into a 120-word international website/profile paragraph with cautious claims.

lessons.title: T2.16 — Working With AI Without Outsourcing Your Thinking [FLEX]
lessons.objectives: FLEX. Define task/context, use AI where appropriate, inspect output, verify claims, revise for audience/purpose, disclose use where required and retain responsibility. Assessment focuses on judgment and verification.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.
lessons.materials:
Linked lesson kit: T2.16 — Working With AI Without Outsourcing Your Thinking [FLEX] — lesson kit
Use the kit’s original input/case and student task sheet; projector plus student notebook/device if permitted.
Support/Core/Stretch routes are embedded in the kit. Use the linked 90-minute POA spine as the default timing model.
lessons.activities:
Retrieval: From T1.12, recall the difference between fluent language and verified evidence.
Output challenge: Show the AI draft without the fact sheet first. Students predict which parts feel trustworthy and why.
Targeted noticing/input: Reveal the fact sheet. Count factual, framing and omission errors separately.
Guided practice: Pairs audit each sentence and agree what must be preserved, corrected, deleted or qualified.
Production 1: Students write the final project-status message and verification log.
Feedback: Partner checks the final text against facts, not against the AI draft.
Improved attempt: Student explains in 45 seconds where AI helped and where human judgment was essential.
Exit ticket: Complete: The most dangerous AI error in this task was ___ because ___.
lessons.homework: Optional FLEX follow-up: preserve one original attempt, AI-assisted version, verification step and final revision from a real low-stakes task permitted by course rules.

lessons.title: T2.17 — Capstone Studio
lessons.objectives: Teams choose or receive a realistic engineering, software, manufacturing, business, research or trade scenario. Build a multi-mode professional communication response.
lessons.framework: Modified Production-Oriented Approach: Motivate → Enable → Produce → Feedback → Reproduce. Shared task with Support/Core/Stretch layers; explicit language work added where performance shows a need.

lessons.activities:
Retrieval: Nine-station self-check across UENG-01–09: teams identify which standards their chosen scenario will visibly evidence.
Output challenge: Teams state the desired audience action/understanding in one sentence before creating any slides.
Targeted noticing/input: Teacher checks alignment: written message, evidence and spoken recommendation must not contradict each other.
Guided practice: Teams build evidence map and rehearsal plan; teacher conferences focus on one highest-risk communication weakness.
Production 1: First full rehearsal with timed transitions and challenge questions.
Feedback: Peer team uses capstone checklist: message, evidence, audience, interaction, professionalism, uncertainty.
Improved attempt: Teams revise one weak component and rerun the relevant 2-minute segment.
Exit ticket: Each student records one personal responsibility for the showcase and one communication risk to practise.

lessons.title: T2.18 — Professional Communication Showcase
lessons.objectives: Capstone performance including concise writing, evidence/data, spoken presentation, interaction/meeting and Q&A. Students must not simply deliver a memorised speech.

resources.title: Course pathway model
resources.notes: Four task-context pathways: Graduate / Research; Industry / Engineering; Business / International; General Development. These are not separate classes.

resources.title: Support / Core / Stretch differentiation guide
resources.notes: Use one shared task with three layers. Support: frames, model language, vocabulary bank, shorter source, preparation time, notes. Core: expected university task. Stretch: less scaffolding, extra source, counterargument, spontaneous Q&A, more technical/professional audience, tighter time.

resources.title: Responsible AI principles
resources.notes: AI may assist. AI output must be checked. The student remains responsible. When appropriate preserve original attempt, AI-assisted version, verification and final human revision.

resources.title: CET-transfer boundary
resources.notes: This is not a CET preparation curriculum. Reading efficiency, vocabulary in context, listening, summarising, writing and argumentation may transfer naturally; optional exam-oriented practice must not consume the main course.

resources.title: 90-minute production-oriented lesson spine
resources.notes: Approximate sequence: 0–10 retrieval/warm-up; 10–20 output challenge; 20–40 targeted input/modelling/noticing; 40–60 guided practice/rehearsal; 60–75 main production; 75–85 feedback; 85–90 improved attempt/exit ticket.

resources.title: University communication activity bank
resources.notes: Reusable low-prep formats. 1) 60-second rebuild: listen/read, close source, reconstruct, verify. 2) Evidence auction: teams spend limited points on the evidence most useful to a claim. 3) Headline first: compress an explanation to one sentence before adding detail. 4) Role rotation: chair / evidence checker / clarifier / summariser. 5) Challenge cards: limitation, counterexample, missing data, audience change. 6) Two-pass production: attempt → one feedback priority → immediate shorter retry. 7) Jargon alarm: listener stops at unexplained specialist language. 8) Decision record: conclusion / evidence / uncertainty / next action. 9) Source relationship sort: agreement / addition / tension / limitation. 10) Audience switch: explain the same content to a novice then a specialist. 11) Verification log: claim / source / cross-check / confidence change. 12) Exit transfer: where will I use this outside today’s lesson?

resources.title: T1.01 — Where Am I Now? — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Diagnostic set. Speaking prompt: Introduce yourself, your major and one situation where you want English to be easier. Reading: a 150-word notice about a student innovation team changing its meeting plan; identify purpose, two key details and one reason. Listening script for teacher read-aloud: a 60-second project update with a deadline, problem and next action. Writing prompt: explain one current English strength and one target in 80–100 words.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Complete four short baseline tasks without coaching. Then choose a primary pathway: Graduate/Research, Industry/Engineering, Business/International or General Development. Finish the sentence: By the end of this year, I want to be able to…

SUPPORT
Allow planning notes, a self-introduction frame and a vocabulary box for major / project / goal / improve.

STRETCH
No script for speaking; add one spontaneous follow-up question and require the written goal to include a measurable success indicator.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
One sentence: The English task I most need to improve is ___ because ___.

resources.title: T1.02 — Read With a Purpose — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Original reading: “Why a Project Team Changed Its Test Plan.” A university robotics team has three weeks before a demo. Their first plan tests every feature equally. After two early failures, the team studies the fault log and moves most testing time to the two functions causing repeated errors. The change does not guarantee success, but it concentrates limited time on the strongest evidence of risk. The team keeps one short full-system test each week to check that solving one problem does not create another.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
1) Skim: write the text’s purpose in 8 words or fewer. 2) Scan: find the time limit and two reasons for the plan change. 3) Structure: label problem → evidence → response → limitation. 4) Evidence check: underline the sentence that best supports the claim that the new plan is evidence-led. 5) Explain the message to a partner without looking at the text.

SUPPORT
Provide the four structure labels in order and a key-word bank: failure, fault log, limited time, concentrate, guarantee.

STRETCH
Write a second plausible interpretation of the same evidence and state what extra information would help decide between them.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write one reading move you used today and when you would use it again.

resources.title: T1.03 — Listen and Capture Meaning — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Teacher read-aloud script: “Project update. We planned to finish the sensor test on Thursday, but one component arrived late. The team can still complete the basic calibration this week. First, Mei will check the replacement component on Friday morning. Then Arjun will run the calibration and upload the results by 5 p.m. The full outdoor test moves to next Tuesday. The important point is that the final demonstration date has not changed. If Friday’s component check fails, we will borrow the older sensor and record the limitation in the report.”

STUDENT TASK SHEET
First listen: write only three headings. Second listen: add keywords under Situation / Change / Next action. Then close your notes for 10 seconds, reopen them and give a 60-second spoken reconstruction. Finish by checking which detail you missed or distorted.

SUPPORT
Give the three headings and permit a symbols bank: → next, ↑ increase, ↓ decrease, ? uncertain, DL deadline.

STRETCH
After the reconstruction, answer: Which detail is most important for a project manager, and why?

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write the one keyword or symbol that helped you recover the most meaning.

resources.title: T1.04 — Say It in Your Own Words — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Source paragraph: “Battery recycling can recover useful materials from cells that are no longer suitable for vehicles. Recovery does not remove every environmental cost: collection, transport and processing also use energy and resources. The value of recycling therefore depends on both the materials recovered and the efficiency of the recovery system.” Sample A copies phrases with small word changes. Sample B changes wording but adds the unsupported claim that recycling is ‘environmentally harmless.’ Sample C accurately condenses the idea and attributes it.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Classify Sample A/B/C as patchwriting, inaccurate paraphrase or acceptable paraphrase. Then write: (a) a 25-word summary, (b) a 45–60 word paraphrase with attribution, and (c) one direct quotation of no more than 8 words embedded in your own sentence.

SUPPORT
Sentence frames: The source explains that…; It also warns that…; According to the source… Provide a synonym-choice bank but require students to change sentence structure too.

STRETCH
Paraphrase for two audiences: a first-year student and a technical project teammate. Preserve meaning while changing emphasis appropriately.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Complete: A paraphrase becomes inaccurate when ___.

resources.title: T1.05 — Make Data Speak — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Fictional classroom dataset — do not treat as real JUST data. A prototype line is tested over four runs. Defect rate: 8.2%, 6.9%, 5.8%, 5.6%. Average cycle time: 41s, 42s, 44s, 47s. Energy per unit: 3.1, 3.0, 3.0, 3.2 kWh. A business-pathway alternative uses the same pattern with returns rate, response time and cost per order.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Prepare a 90-second data update with four moves: current pattern, strongest comparison, cautious interpretation, next question/action. You must use at least two numbers and may not claim that one trend caused another unless the dataset proves it.

SUPPORT
Language bank: rose/fell from…to…; remained broadly stable; by contrast; may indicate; we cannot conclude; the next step is to check…

STRETCH
Include one limitation and answer a challenge question that asks whether the apparent improvement is worth the trade-off.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write one claim the data supports and one claim it does not support.

resources.title: T1.06 — Build an Argument — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Decision case: A student project course is considering a rule requiring every team to hold a 15-minute progress meeting each week. Evidence card 1: teams often discover coordination problems late. Evidence card 2: some teams already communicate frequently online. Evidence card 3: fixed meetings can become ritual updates with little value. Evidence card 4: short meetings can expose blocked tasks early. No card proves the policy is universally good or bad.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Build a position using Claim → Reason → Evidence → Qualification/Counterpoint. Then swap sides and build the strongest opposing position. Mark each sentence F (fact/evidence), I (interpretation), O (opinion) or A (assumption).

SUPPORT
Frame: I think ___ because ___. The strongest evidence is ___. However, ___. Therefore, a reasonable policy would be ___.

STRETCH
Add a condition under which your recommendation would change and identify what new evidence would matter most.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write the assumption in your own argument that most needs checking.

resources.title: T1.07 — Source-Based Position — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Assessment source set (original). Reading: a 180-word proposal says a faculty should replace some live project briefings with recorded updates to reduce scheduling conflicts; it notes that recordings improve access but may reduce immediate questioning. Listening: teacher reads a 75-second response from a project supervisor arguing that live questioning reveals misunderstandings quickly, while accepting that recordings are useful for routine status updates.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Prepare an approximately two-minute position answering: How should the faculty use recorded and live project updates? Use both sources. Include one qualification. After feedback, make a shorter revised attempt.

SUPPORT
Give a two-column source grid and structure cards: position / source A / source B / qualification / conclusion. Notes allowed; no full script.

STRETCH
Integrate the sources by relationship (agreement, tension, limitation) rather than discussing them one at a time. Take one spontaneous question.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write exactly what you changed between attempt 1 and attempt 2.

resources.title: T1.08 — Academic Discussion — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Discussion case: A fictional student innovation fund has 20,000 RMB left. Proposal A: buy shared sensors used by six engineering teams. Proposal B: fund translation/design support for teams entering an international competition. Proposal C: extend evening access to a prototyping room. Proposal D: run an industry mentor event. Each has benefits, unknowns and different beneficiaries.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
In groups of four, allocate the full budget across at least two proposals. Everyone must enter the discussion, invite another speaker once, ask for evidence/clarification once and disagree or qualify appropriately once. Produce a one-minute final rationale.

SUPPORT
Function cards: Can I add…?; What evidence do we have for…?; I agree up to a point…; Could you clarify…?; We have not heard from…; So are we saying…?

STRETCH
Assign a rotating chair who must surface disagreement and test whether the final decision reflects evidence rather than the loudest speaker.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Who helped the discussion move forward today, and what exactly did they do?

resources.title: T1.09 — Explain Your Major to Me — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Audience challenge. Explain one major-related item to an intelligent non-specialist: engineering students may choose a robot subsystem, EV component, additive-manufacturing step or metallurgical process; software students a data flow or feature; business/trade students a supply-chain step, pricing model or transaction process. Audience card: ‘I am educated, but I do not study your field. I will stop you whenever you use an unexplained specialist term.’

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Build a 2–3 minute explanation using Purpose → Parts/Steps → Example → Why it matters. Define no more than three essential technical terms. Use one analogy, comparison or concrete example. Then answer two audience questions.

SUPPORT
Planning grid and frames: It is used to…; The process has three main stages…; In simple terms…; For example…; The important point is…

STRETCH
Explain the same idea twice: once to a non-specialist and once to a knowledgeable peer. Identify what changes in detail, terminology and assumed knowledge.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write one piece of assumed knowledge you removed from your explanation.

resources.title: T1.10 — Present Clearly — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Presentation design cards. Weak opening: ‘Today I will introduce my topic.’ Stronger opening states the problem/value. Weak slide: 8 lines of sentences. Stronger slide: one claim, one visual/data point and a short label. Delivery problem cards: reading, no signposting, rushing, facing screen, ending without a conclusion.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Prepare a 3-minute mini-presentation with 3–5 slides or equivalent visual cues. Required moves: meaningful opening, clear roadmap/signposting, 2–3 main points, conclusion that answers ‘so what?’, and one audience question. Slides must not contain paragraph scripts.

SUPPORT
Provide a slide skeleton and signposts: First…; The key point here is…; This matters because…; To sum up…

STRETCH
Remove most written cues and handle a 45-second Q&A. Use one visual that the audience must interpret rather than merely decorate.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write the sentence you want the audience to remember tomorrow.

resources.title: T1.11 — Combine Sources — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Source A (reading): recorded lectures let students pause difficult explanations and revisit terminology, but passive rewatching does not guarantee learning. Source B (teacher read-aloud): a student describes using short recordings after class, but says the biggest benefit comes from pausing to write a question and then checking the answer in notes or with classmates. The sources overlap but emphasise different mechanisms.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Create a synthesis that organises ideas by relationship, not source order. Use at least three connectors from: similarly, both, however, whereas, in addition, this limits, taken together. Produce either a 120–150 word synthesis or a 90-second spoken version.

SUPPORT
Venn grid: shared idea / Source A only / Source B only / relationship. Sentence frame: Both sources suggest ___. However, A emphasises ___, whereas B adds ___.

STRETCH
Add a cautious inference that follows from both sources, and label it clearly as an inference rather than a source claim.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Complete: Synthesis is different from two summaries because ___.

resources.title: T1.12 — Can I Trust This? — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Simulated claim-check set. Claim 1 comes from a named university lab page dated this year and links to its method. Claim 2 appears in an undated repost with no author. Claim 3 is an AI-generated paragraph containing a precise statistic but no traceable source. Claim 4 is an older official report that is credible but may not answer today’s question. Claim 5 cites a primary dataset but overstates what correlation proves.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
For each claim, record: Who says it? What evidence? When? Relevant to this question? Primary/secondary? What independent check would you make? Verdict options: usable, usable with limitation, not yet verified, unsupported. The verdict must include reasoning.

SUPPORT
Use the VERIFY grid: Voice/author, Evidence, Recency, Independence, Fit/relevance, Your cross-check.

STRETCH
Two apparently credible sources disagree. Design a verification plan that prioritises primary evidence and explains what would make you change your view.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write the sentence: ‘I would not trust this yet because…’ using a concrete reason, not ‘because it is AI.’

resources.title: T1.13 — Explain China Across Cultures — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Audience scenario: an international visitor has never studied at a Chinese university and asks about one local/campus practice. Options include QR-based daily services, a university club/recruitment event, a Zhangjiagang public-space feature, high-speed rail travel, a local manufacturing context or a discipline-specific Chinese example. The visitor is curious, not ignorant; avoid ‘Chinese people always…’ explanations.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Prepare a 2-minute explainer using Context → What happens → Why/when it matters → Comparison only if useful → Check understanding. Identify two things your audience may not know and define them before they become a barrier. Take two follow-up questions.

SUPPORT
Frames: In this context…; You may not be familiar with…; It is similar to ___, but…; This is common in ___ situations, although…

STRETCH
Explain to two audience cards with different prior knowledge. Remove stereotypes and over-generalised claims; add a limitation or variation.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
What did you know so well that you forgot your audience might not know it?

resources.title: T1.14 — Integrated Academic Challenge — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Integrated challenge (fictional). Campus food outlets want to reduce single-use takeaway packaging without increasing average service time too much. Source A: short student survey summary says convenience is the main reason for takeaway use. Source B: operations note says reusable-container returns create cleaning and storage work. Source C: small fictional table compares three pilot options on cost, estimated waste reduction and average extra service seconds. None is clearly best on every measure.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Teams must recommend one pilot for a six-week trial. Use all three sources, identify one limitation, discuss alternatives, prepare a 3-minute recommendation and answer questions. Submit a one-page evidence map rather than a full report.

SUPPORT
Evidence map columns: decision criterion / source evidence / what it suggests / limitation. Presentation frame: recommendation first → evidence → trade-off → next check.

STRETCH
Add one stakeholder objection, quantify a trade-off from the table and propose a success metric that could falsify your recommendation.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Which earlier Term 1 skill mattered most in today’s challenge, and where did you use it?

resources.title: T1.15 — Academic Communication Showcase — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Showcase evidence set: selected baseline prompt from T1.01, one source/data task, one prepared academic communication task, Q&A prompts, and portfolio reflection grid. Students compare evidence rather than relying on memory of improvement.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Complete the capstone performance and one repeated baseline task. Then select two artefacts: one that shows strongest growth and one that reveals a next priority. Reflection prompts: What changed? What evidence proves it? What still breaks down under pressure? What will transfer into Term 2?

SUPPORT
Allow structured planning grid and chosen portfolio evidence. Reflection sentence frames focus on evidence: In September I…, now I…, the clearest evidence is…

STRETCH
Add spontaneous Q&A and require a transfer claim: how will one academic communication skill be used in research, industry or professional contexts?

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Finish: ‘In Term 2 I want to transfer ___ into ___, and I will know it is improving when ___.’

resources.title: T2.01 — Reactivate and Transfer — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Transfer profile card. Build a 90-second answer to three questions: Who am I? What do I study / work on? Where am I going next? The answer must include one concrete project/skill example and one current English goal. Avoid a list of subjects or adjectives without evidence.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Give the profile once from memory, then map which Term 1 abilities are reusable in professional contexts: explaining, evidence, data, discussion, source judgment, presentation and Q&A. Update your pathway only if your goal has genuinely changed.

SUPPORT
Frame: I study…; One project that shows this is…; I am interested in…; The English skill I most need for that is…

STRETCH
Deliver the same profile to two audience cards: a postgraduate supervisor and an employer. Change detail, evidence and emphasis without changing facts.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Which Term 1 skill will matter most in your current pathway this term?

resources.title: T2.02 — Tell Your Skills Story — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Evidence statements. Weak: ‘I am a good team player.’ Stronger: ‘In a four-person design project, I coordinated weekly task updates and combined test results into the final briefing.’ Weak: ‘I know Python.’ Stronger: ‘I used Python to clean and compare three weeks of sensor data, then explained the pattern to my team.’

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Create four evidence statements for skills you may use in a CV, profile or interview. Each must contain Action + Context + Result/Value. At least two statements should come from real study/project experience, not personality labels.

SUPPORT
Verb bank: analysed, designed, coordinated, tested, compared, presented, resolved, improved, documented, negotiated. Frame: In ___, I ___, which helped ___ / resulted in ___.

STRETCH
Write one statement for a technical reader and one for a non-technical recruiter. Keep evidence constant but adapt terminology and value.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Circle the statement you could defend most confidently in an interview.

resources.title: T2.03 — Interview Communication — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Interview question bank by pathway. General: Tell me about a project you are proud of. Describe a time something did not go to plan. Why are you interested in this opportunity? Engineering/software: Explain a technical problem you helped solve. Business/trade: Describe a decision you made with incomplete information. Research: Tell me about a question you want to investigate.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Answer using Direct answer → Situation → Task → Action → Result/Learning. Keep context short and spend most time on your own action. Practise one known question and one unexpected follow-up.

SUPPORT
STAR cue card plus rescue phrases: Let me think for a moment; The part I was responsible for was…; I do not know that yet, but I would check…

STRETCH
Answer without visible STAR headings and handle two follow-ups that challenge your evidence or ask what you would do differently.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
What follow-up question exposed the weakest part of your evidence?

resources.title: T2.04 — Professional Email and Messaging — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Message repair set. Example bad email: ‘Teacher hello. I cannot come tomorrow because something happened. Please tell me what I miss. Thanks.’ Context cards specify audience, purpose and constraint: professor requesting a deadline clarification; supervisor confirming a changed meeting; recruiter following up after an interview; client/partner asking for missing information.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Write two messages for different audiences. Each must use a useful subject line, purpose in the first 1–2 sentences, necessary context, clear requested action/next step and appropriate close. Maximum 120 words each unless the task genuinely needs more.

SUPPORT
Template: Subject → purpose → essential context → request/action → thanks/close. Phrase bank for requests, confirmation and follow-up.

STRETCH
Rewrite one message for a more senior or more familiar audience and explain two tone changes. Remove 20% of words without losing meaning.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write the strongest subject line you created and why it works.

resources.title: T2.05 — Meetings That Achieve Something — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Meeting case: A project team is two weeks from a demo. One task is complete, one is blocked by missing data, one depends on another teammate, and one risk has no owner. The team has 8 minutes to agree what happens next. Agenda: progress → blockers → decisions → actions.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Run a short meeting and produce an action record with Decision / Owner / Deadline / Open question. Each participant must give one update, ask/answer one clarification question and help summarise a decision.

SUPPORT
Function bank: My update is…; The blocker is…; What do you need from…?; Can we decide…?; So the action is… and ___ owns it by ___.

STRETCH
Chair the meeting without dominating it. Surface one hidden dependency and close with a concise verbal summary from memory.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Which sentence moved the meeting from discussion to action?

resources.title: T2.06 — Solve a Problem Together — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Problem set with pathway choices. Engineering: a critical component fails final testing and replacement takes five days. Software: a release has a reproducible bug affecting one key workflow. Business/trade: a supplier delay threatens a client deadline. Research: a dataset has missing values in one key variable. Teams receive evidence cards, constraints and three imperfect options.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Use Diagnose → Options → Criteria → Compare → Decide → Risk. Produce a team recommendation with rationale and one contingency. You must explicitly reject at least one plausible option and explain why.

SUPPORT
Decision matrix with three criteria; phrases: The immediate problem is…; Option A is stronger on… but weaker on…; We recommend… because…; If ___ happens, we will…

STRETCH
Introduce a late evidence card that changes one criterion. Teams must decide whether to keep or revise the recommendation and explain why.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
What information would most reduce uncertainty in your decision?

resources.title: T2.07 — Explain a Product, Process or System — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
System explanation cards. Engineering: regenerative braking, robotic pick-and-place cell, additive-manufacturing workflow. Software: login request flow, recommendation pipeline, bug-report lifecycle. Business/trade: order-to-delivery process, customer return process, import/export documentation flow. Students may substitute a real major topic.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Explain one product/process/system to a non-specialist using Need/Purpose → Inputs → Main stages/components → Output → Failure/limit → Why it matters. Use one simple diagram or hand-drawn flow.

SUPPORT
Sequence language and definition frames; limit specialist terms to five and require plain-language definitions.

STRETCH
Audience asks one ‘what if this part fails?’ question and one ‘why not use an alternative?’ question. Student answers with appropriate uncertainty.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Which specialist term did you decide was essential, and how did you define it?

resources.title: T2.08 — Precision Matters — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Ambiguity cards. Engineering instruction: ‘Tighten the unit and restart it when it looks stable.’ Business process: ‘Send the documents quickly and confirm with the customer if needed.’ Software: ‘Check the failed jobs and rerun the important ones.’ Each lacks measurable conditions, sequence, ownership or risk limits.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Rewrite one procedure using ordered steps, explicit conditions, measurable thresholds where appropriate and a stop/clarify rule. Then give the instructions orally while a partner deliberately asks clarification questions.

SUPPORT
Frames: Before…, check…; If X is above/below…, then…; Do not… until…; Stop and confirm if…; The final check is…

STRETCH
Write for a high-risk or high-cost context. Add one exception and explain why over-specific instructions can also fail when conditions change.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write one word from today that should trigger you to ask ‘what exactly does that mean?’

resources.title: T2.09 — Give a Data Update — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Fictional update dataset. Option A engineering: output 920→970 units/week; defect rate 3.8%→3.1%; unplanned downtime 4.2→5.0 hours. Option B software: active users +12%; crash rate 1.8%→1.2%; average support response 5.4→6.1 hours. Option C business: orders +9%; on-time delivery 94%→91%; returns stable at 2.4%.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Give a 90-second update in this order: headline/current state → important change → significance → uncertainty/trade-off → next action. Use numbers selectively; do not narrate every value.

SUPPORT
Headline frames: Overall…; The main improvement is…; The concern is…; We do not yet know…; Next we should…

STRETCH
Audience challenges whether the headline is too positive/negative. Defend the framing and state what extra metric would change it.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Which number did you deliberately leave out, and why?

resources.title: T2.10 — Make a Recommendation — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Recommendation case. A project team must choose how to share weekly progress with an overseas partner. Option A: long weekly report; B: 15-minute live call + one-page action note; C: asynchronous dashboard + monthly call. Constraints: 6-hour time-zone difference, partner wants quick risk visibility, team has limited admin time, some issues need discussion.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Use SCQA: Situation (shared project) → Complication (visibility + time-zone/admin constraints) → Question (best communication setup?) → Answer (recommendation first). Produce a 150-word recommendation or 90-second spoken proposal with two reasons and one limitation.

SUPPORT
SCQA planning boxes and answer-first frame: We recommend ___ because __ and __. This works best if ___.

STRETCH
Add implementation detail: first 30 days, success metric and a condition that would trigger a change of approach.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write your Answer sentence only. It must be actionable.

resources.title: T2.11 — Defend Your Recommendation — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Challenge panel cards: 1) Your evidence is too limited. 2) What is the biggest downside? 3) Why not option B? 4) What would make you change your recommendation? 5) You gave a number—where did it come from? 6) We cannot implement this now; what is the minimum viable next step? 7) I do not understand the technical term you used.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Present a 60–90 second recommendation from T2.10 or a new case, then answer 3–5 challenge cards. Use Direct answer → Reason/evidence → Limitation/next check when needed. ‘I don’t know’ is acceptable only if followed by what you would verify.

SUPPORT
Response stems: The short answer is…; The evidence we have is…; That is a real limitation…; I do not know that yet; I would check…

STRETCH
Panel may interrupt, reframe or challenge an assumption. Student must stay concise and correct themselves explicitly if needed.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write one sentence you can use when you genuinely do not know an answer.

resources.title: T2.12 — International Workplace Communication — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Workplace interaction repairs. Scenario A: a teammate says ‘This plan is impossible’ in a meeting; another hears it as personal criticism. B: a manager says ‘It would be good to have this soon’; a new team member interprets no deadline. C: a junior colleague notices a likely error but avoids questioning a senior person. D: feedback says ‘Maybe you can improve the report a little,’ but the required changes are major. Avoid explaining these as fixed national traits.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
For two scenarios, identify the pragmatic problem, rewrite the interaction and add a clarification move that reduces assumptions. Discuss how role, relationship, urgency, medium and individual preference may matter.

SUPPORT
Repair language: When you say ___, do you mean…?; My concern is with the plan, not the person; Could we agree a specific deadline?; I may be missing something, but…

STRETCH
Create two valid repair strategies with different levels of directness and explain when each might be appropriate.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Complete: When communication feels indirect/direct, I should first check ___ rather than assume ___.

resources.title: T2.13 — Professional Networking [FLEX] — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Networking role cards. Student researcher seeking someone working on similar methods; engineering student at an industry open day; software student meeting a product engineer; trade/business student at a supplier event; general student at an international campus event. Each card includes one useful thing to learn and one thing you can offer/share.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Run three 3-minute conversations. Required moves: natural introduction, one open question, follow-up based on the answer, concise self/skills explanation, useful exchange, polite exit. Do not turn the interaction into an interview questionnaire.

SUPPORT
Openers/exits: What brings you here?; I’m working on…; That’s interesting—how does…?; It was useful hearing about…; I’m going to…, but may I…?

STRETCH
Join a conversation already in progress and exit without abruptness. Summarise the other person’s interest accurately afterward.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write one follow-up question that made a conversation feel genuinely connected.

resources.title: T2.14 — Research and Postgraduate Communication — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Research communication set. Mini abstract structure: Background/problem → Aim/question → Method/approach → Main result or expected contribution → Significance/limit. Poster pitch audience: an academic from a neighbouring field, not your exact specialty. Contact-email case: ask a potential supervisor a focused question after reading their work, not a generic ‘please accept me’ message.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Choose a real or plausible project/research interest. Produce a 90-second poster/research-interest pitch and a 100-word contact message. The pitch must state the question/problem and why it matters before technical detail.

SUPPORT
Pitch frame: I’m interested in… because…; The specific question is…; My current approach is…; The main challenge is…; I want to investigate…

STRETCH
Take two research questions from the audience: one about method/evidence, one about limitation/next step. Adapt explanation to a neighbouring discipline.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Write your research/project question in one sentence without vague nouns like ‘development’ or ‘application’ unless defined.

resources.title: T2.15 — Take Your Local Expertise Global [FLEX] — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Local expertise options: explain a JUST/Zhangjiagang/Suzhou-Jiangsu industrial context, a Chinese company/innovation case you know, a manufacturing/trade process, or a discipline-specific development. Audience card has no local background and may not know institutional names, policy labels or why the example matters internationally.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Create a 2-minute international-facing explainer with Context → Specific example → Significance → Connection to wider field → Limitation/variation. Define local names and avoid promotional claims you cannot support.

SUPPORT
Context frames: ___ is located/used in…; For someone unfamiliar with the area…; A useful way to understand it is…; One reason it matters beyond the local context is…

STRETCH
Audience challenges whether your example is representative. Respond with a limitation and distinguish one case from a national/general claim.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Which local term/name needed the most context, and what definition worked?

resources.title: T2.16 — Working With AI Without Outsourcing Your Thinking [FLEX] — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
AI verification case. Original task: write a concise project-status message from five verified facts. A simulated AI draft is fluent but (a) changes one deadline, (b) invents a ‘15% improvement’, (c) makes the tone more certain than the evidence, and (d) omits one unresolved risk. Students receive the verified fact sheet and the AI draft.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Use Define → Context → Generate/assist → Inspect → Verify → Revise → Disclose → Own. Mark every draft sentence as supported / unsupported / misleading / style-only. Produce a corrected final message plus a short verification log.

SUPPORT
Verification table: AI sentence / supporting fact / issue / correction. Disclosure frame if required: I used AI to help with ___; I verified/revised ___.

STRETCH
Ask AI (simulated or permitted tool) for a second version with a different audience. Compare not only factual accuracy but judgment, tone and omitted uncertainty.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Complete: The most dangerous AI error in this task was ___ because ___.

resources.title: T2.17 — Capstone Studio — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Capstone scenario bank. 1 Engineering: brief an overseas partner on a quality problem and recovery plan. 2 Software: propose a workflow change after user complaints and system metrics. 3 Manufacturing: explain a recurring defect, evidence and corrective trial. 4 Business: recommend an international market-entry pilot with risks. 5 Research: present preliminary findings and next study step. 6 Trade/client: respond to a delayed shipment while preserving the relationship. All scenarios require writing + evidence/data + spoken explanation + interaction/Q&A.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Teams choose/receive one scenario and create a communication package: one concise written item, one evidence visual/table, a 4–5 minute spoken briefing, a meeting/interaction segment and Q&A preparation. Assign roles but ensure every member speaks and owns evidence.

SUPPORT
Capstone canvas: audience / decision or outcome / known facts / unknowns / message / evidence / risk / written item / speaking roles / likely questions.

STRETCH
Add one realistic constraint halfway through studio time: changed deadline, new data, stakeholder objection or resource cut. Teams must update the package coherently.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Each student records one personal responsibility for the showcase and one communication risk to practise.

resources.title: T2.18 — Professional Communication Showcase — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Showcase protocol. Each team submits/uses: concise written communication, one evidence/data element, 4–5 minute briefing, 2–3 minute interaction/meeting or decision segment, and Q&A. Assessors use linked rubrics; memorised speech without responsive interaction cannot fully evidence the task.

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Deliver the professional communication capstone. Every student must contribute to at least two modes across the package and answer or handle interaction. Preserve team evidence plus individual reflection notes.

SUPPORT
Allow role cards, keyword notes and visible action/evidence structure. Do not require memorised scripts.

STRETCH
Additional panel question tests limitation, alternative, implementation or evidence source. Strong students must remain concise rather than adding length.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Individual: Which part of the performance best proves usable professional English rather than memorisation?

resources.title: T2.19 — Evidence of Growth — lesson kit
resources.notes:
CORE INPUT / CASE
Growth evidence grid. Columns: baseline evidence (T1.01), mid-year evidence, capstone/end evidence, observable change, remaining weakness, next context. Prompts focus on performance: Can I explain? understand? verify? discuss? write? present? interact? use AI responsibly? improve from feedback?

STUDENT TASK SHEET
Select 3–5 artefacts across the year. For each, write one evidence claim: ‘Earlier I…, now I…, shown by…’. Identify one persistent weakness and an independent strategy with a trigger/cadence. Finish the final task: What can I now do in English that I could not do confidently before?

SUPPORT
Reflection frames tied to evidence rather than feelings. Allow students to use rubric/competency matrix labels and teacher comments.

STRETCH
Write a transfer plan for a real next-stage context (CET support, postgraduate research, internship, technical work, international business) with one measurable 8-week target.

FEEDBACK / EXIT
Final sentence: In the next 8 weeks, I will ___ in English ___ times / by ___, because my evidence shows ___.
